title: How The 'Venice' Epycs Measure Up Against Prior AMD Server CPUs
gist: AMD's sixth-gen 'Venice' Epyc launches with 31 SKUs (8-256 cores, up to $14,904) across new SP7 and SP8 sockets, Zen 6 cores on TSMC 2nm with a 20% IPC gain, and I/O dies kept on 6nm. Morgan's historical comparison shows the 256-core SP7 top part delivering 190X the performance of a 2008 Opteron at 14.9X better price/performance, with AMD pressing Intel and positioning against hyperscaler Arm CPUs.

insights.claim: AMD's sixth-generation 'Venice' Epyc server CPU line launches with 31 SKUs spanning 8 to 256 cores, 130 to 600 watts, and $700 to $14,904 list price in 1,000-unit trays.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The breadth of the stack (two sockets, two I/O dies, two compute dies) lets AMD target nearly every datacenter workload tier against Intel and Arm.
insights.locator: With the “Venice” generation of Epyc chips that launch today

insights.claim: The Epyc 9G76 is a Venice SP7 SKU built specifically for AMD's Helion AI racks and is barely different from the HPC-oriented Epyc 9686F; the author believes they are kept distinct so hyperscalers and cloud builders can be discounted more heavily than HPC centers.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Signals volume-driven price discrimination in favor of hyperscalers; list prices overstate realized ASPs on AI-rack CPU sales.
insights.quote: The hyperscalers and cloud builders are no doubt going to get better deals than the HPC centers of the world, given the high volumes they are purchasing.
insights.locator: By the way, the Epyc 9G76 processor

insights.claim: Venice SP8-socket mainstream CPUs (22 variants) will not ship until the first half of 2027 per AMD, with the author guessing early in the year; the nine SP7 parts are shipping now.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Mainstream-volume Venice revenue ramps in 2027; near-term Venice revenue is concentrated in high-end SP7 parts.
insights.locator: The SP8 socket versions of the Venice CPUs will not ship until next year

insights.claim: In Venice, AMD stopped splitting Zen 6 and Zen 6c into distinct families; both keep the same cache hierarchy and differ only in scheduler optimization for high-core/low-clock versus low-core/high-clock CCDs.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Removes the cache-sensitive performance penalty of dense cores, making the high-core-count parts more broadly deployable.
insights.locator: Rather than keep the Zen 6 and Zen 6c designs

insights.claim: With Turin's Zen 5c, AMD halved L3 cache per CCD to fit more cores, which hurt cache-sensitive workloads — a trade-off the Venice design avoids.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Explains why dense-core Venice parts may outperform Turin dense parts disproportionately on cache-heavy workloads.
insights.locator: With the prior Turin Zen 5c cores

insights.claim: Venice uses a 12-core CCD with 48 MB of L3 and a 32-core CCD with 128 MB of L3, both made on TSMC 2 nanometer processes.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: AMD is a leading-edge TSMC 2nm customer for server CPUs, relevant to TSMC N2 demand.
insights.locator: Both the 12-core CCD, which has 48 MB of L3 cache

insights.claim: AMD says Zen 6 delivers an average 20 percent integer IPC uplift per core at the same clock versus Zen 5, which the author calls a relatively big generational jump.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Per-core gains compound with core-count increases, widening AMD's throughput lead over Intel.
insights.locator: This time around, the average performance uplift per core

insights.claim: Both Venice I/O dies (SP7 and SP8) stay on TSMC 6 nanometer because I/O does not shrink as well as compute, and shrinking it makes signaling harder and costs more.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Chiplet disaggregation keeps leading-edge wafer spend focused on compute dies, supporting AMD's cost structure and mature-node TSMC demand.
insights.quote: there is not a lot of benefit from using the most advanced processes to etch I/O and other signaling chiplets because I/O does not shrink as well as compute does
insights.locator: This SP7 socket I/O (and memory) die

insights.claim: The Venice SP7 socket offers 16 DDR5 channels delivering up to 1.6 TB/sec with 12.8 GT/sec MRDIMMs (1 TB/sec with 8 GT/sec RDIMMs), up to 512 GB per stick, plus 96 PCI-Express 6.0 lanes and eight PCIe 4.0 lanes.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Memory bandwidth leap favors MRDIMM adoption and memory-bound AI/HPC workloads; a tailwind for high-capacity DRAM module demand.
insights.locator: The SP7 socket, which is shipping now

insights.claim: The mainstream Venice SP8 socket halves memory bandwidth versus SP7 (eight DDR5 channels, two DIMMs per channel) but offers 33 percent more I/O with 128 PCI-Express 6.0 lanes, exposing 192 lanes in a two-socket setup.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: SP8 is positioned for I/O-heavy configurations (accelerators, storage, networking) rather than memory-bound throughput.
insights.quote: So, half the memory bandwidth but 33 percent more I/O.
insights.locator: Moving on to the SP8 socket

insights.claim: The top-bin Epyc 9996 SP7 (256 cores) delivers about 190X the performance of the 2008 Opteron 2393 SE at 14.9X lower cost per unit of performance, while costing 12.8X as much per chip.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: AMD captures higher chip ASPs while still improving customer value — supportive of server CPU revenue growth via consolidation, agentic AI and HPC demand.
insights.locator: The net result is that the Epyc 9996 SP7 part

insights.claim: The Venice Epyc 9746 SP8 delivers 108.2X the performance of the Opteron 2393 SE, 10.8X better bang for the buck, at a 10X higher chip price.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: SP8 carries a price premium per unit of performance versus SP7, steering cost-sensitive throughput buyers to SP7.
insights.locator: For the Venice Epyc 9746 SP8 chip

insights.claim: Top-bin Epyc performance has scaled roughly linearly from Naples through Venice SP8, but the 256-core Venice SP7 is an outlier that jumps throughput onto an exponential trajectory.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The SP7 part is the standout for throughput-oriented buyers and server consolidation economics.
insights.locator: As is immediately obvious in the chart above

insights.claim: AMD's price/performance gains were steep with Rome (first chiplet design with separate compute tiles and I/O die), slowed with Milan and Genoa, and accelerated again with Turin and Venice, especially rewarding SP7 throughput buyers.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: AMD is again using aggressive value to take share, rather than maximizing per-unit margin capture.
insights.locator: What you can also see is how aggressively AMD moved

insights.claim: AMD charges a slight premium for Venice SP8 parts with half the cores at somewhat higher clocks because clock speed adds heat faster than adding cores after a process shrink.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Expect frequency-optimized SKUs to carry persistently worse price/performance than core-dense SKUs.
insights.quote: Clock speed is always going to come at a premium because that adds heat faster than increasing cores after a process shrink.
insights.locator: AMD is charging a slight premium for the SP8 versions

insights.claim: AMD keeps gaining server CPU share every quarter against Intel, and the author finds it surprising Intel has held the share it still has.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Continued share shift toward AMD in x86 servers; Intel's remaining share looks fragile to the author.
insights.quote: It is a wonder that Intel has been able to hold onto the market share is does get, to be honest.
insights.locator: Bad timing for AMD, good timing for Intel.

insights.claim: AMD must keep raising the bar because the Arm collective is rising among hyperscalers and cloud builders, who account for half of the server market.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The key long-term threat to AMD server share is in-house/Arm CPUs at hyperscalers, not Intel.
insights.quote: AMD is not only keeping the heat on Intel. It is turning it up.
insights.locator: AMD is not only keeping the heat on Intel.

insights.claim: The 2008 Shanghai Opterons were AMD's last competitive Opterons; Intel's Nehalem Xeon 5500, which borrowed heavily from AMD's designs, arrived as the Great Recession began and AMD stumbled.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Historical context for how execution slips let Intel regain dominance — the window AMD now aims not to leave open.
insights.locator: These were pretty much the last competitive Opterons
